article.title: Socialism Deferred: The Communist Party of Italy and the Historic Compromise of 1976
article.author: Socialist Forum
article.content: American politics is at a crossroads. All that was once considered certain or possible is now in question. For the first time since the early 20th century, American Socialists are gaining considerable municipal and state level influence through successful and highly publicized electoral campaigns. After a largely successful midterm showing, the DSA established itself as a small but potent force in American politics. For the first time there is a comparatively large cohort of elected DSA members holding local, state, and federal office. Along with this heightened political influence comes greater political risk. Questions of electoral positioning and maneuver take on greater weight. Examining the past experience of socialist and non-socialist alliances can be instructive. Italy provides a pertinent example of a large socialist party, the Italian Communist Party (PCI), that entered an election in 1976 that seemed to have it poised on the precipice of entering government for the first time since the onset of the cold war. This did not occur. Instead, it offers an example of the critical importance of electoral strategy, social research, and ideological flexibility. Despite a major electoral breakthrough with a historic 34% of the vote in 1976, the Italian Communist Party (PCI) was unable to translate this into a wider challenge to the institutional and economic order in Italy. The Communist Party benefitted from the leadership of Chairman Enrico Berlinguer, widely recognized as a particularly charismatic and talented politician. He and his associates pursued a strategic alliance with the Christian Democrats known as the Historic Compromise to bolster future electoral efforts. In reality the compromise undermined the long-term viability of the PCI project. Its failure stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of the mandate delivered by voters as well as a failure to anticipate the political realities of being a subordinate non-governing party to the Christian Democrats. At no point did the DC share power with the PCI. The party agreed initially to a non-sfiducia regime, meaning it promised not to call for a vote of no confidence. Ultimately, the PCI endorsed the government under long-serving and known conservative Christian Democratic Prime Minister Giuliio Andreotti in 1978 even though the party was denied any ministerial positions. Transitioning from the no-confidence regime to the “National Solidarity Government” the PCI still did not receive a meaningful stake in national power. Forced to defend unpopular measures, it ultimately entered the next election of 1979 in a worse position, presaging a process of decline throughout the 1980s and ultimate dissolution in 1991. the cold war dilemma of the pci The Italian Communist Party in 1976 was a mass based electoral Socialist Party confronted by the harsh political realities of the Cold War. It was viewed by many in the center and on the right as an agent of Moscow, functioning to subvert the democratic order. Simultaneously, to many Italian workers, peasants, and increasingly large shares of the petty bourgeoisie as well as students, the Italian Communist Party was a vehicle to advance democratic struggles that ranged from the armed resistance to Fascism to the right to divorce. Berlinguer and the leadership of the PCI correctly viewed their reliance on the Soviet Union as an obstacle to the democratic transfer of power. They formulated a new political line to demonstrate that the Party was a responsible democratic institution while also remaining faithful to the class struggle. Having its foundation in longserving leader of the Party and prominent Communist International Official, Palmiro Togliatti’s, recognition of Parliament as a legitimate vehicle for class struggle and his belief that there were multiple national roads to socialism, the line adopted by the PCI came to be known as “Eurocommunism” (a view adopted in different ways by the French, Spanish, and Italian Communist parties). Eurocommunism revolved around the idea that it was possible to utilize the parliament of bourgeois republics to peacefully transition from capitalism to socialism. This perspective tied all three parties (though the French would eventually break with Eurocommunism) to electoralism. This raises a basic problem: how does one retain the revolutionary goals and impetus of Socialism while supporting a bourgeois electoral process? The ideological basis of the Historic Compromise was established by Berlinguer in a series of articles released in the main party newspaper and official organ, Rinascita. Berlinguer was starting from a position of perennial opposition to not only the DC, but the entire spectrum of “bourgeois ideology”. To accomplish the ideological shift, he separated, in line with Italian historic experience, anti-Imperialism from absolute anticapitalism: “It is the duty of communists and all who fight for the cause of democratic progress and of the liberation of the people to raise the level of consciousness regarding these truths, in order to direct vigilant attention to all of the threats that imperialism and the ruling bourgeois class poses to the freedom of people and independence of nations.” (1) This opened the line of reasoning that would allow a Party militant or longtime supporter to consider that the cause of democratic progress writ large may constitute sufficient ideological similarity to the Communist commitment to anti-Fascism, thus to allow for the Communists to stand in alliance. This was not sufficient, however. To confront decades of inherited bias against accommodation with the DC, Berlinguer sought to employ one of the most potent symbols of the PCI, the Resistenza. Referencing the Salerno Turn when the Kingdom of Italy joined the Allies in World War Two through an agreement of all of the Anti-Fascist forces in the country, he wrote, “The more profound sense of the turn (at Salerno) was the necessity and the desire of the Communist Party to come to terms with all of Italian history, and with all of the historic forces (Socialists, Catholics, and others with democratic inspirations) who were present on the national scene and who fought alongside us for democracy, for national independence, and unity.” (2) By invoking the broad anti-fascist front of wartime, he was suggesting it might be reconstituted in the present. Berlinguer concluded, “If it is true that a democratic renewal can only be realized if it is supported by vast majority of the population, there is not only a need for a policy of large social alliances but also a determined system of political agreements that fosters a convergence and collaboration between all of democratic and popular forces until there is realized a political alliance among them.” (3) This justified the fundamental political logic of the historic compromise, that it was acceptable for the PCI to explore uniting with non-Communist forces to oppose Imperialism, that there were historic forces in the country (Socialism, Catholics, others) who could be united with today because of their role in the historic anti-fascist struggle, and that a revolutionary democratic program can only be pursued through a system of large social and political alliances. What Berlinguer did not anticipate was that the convergence he spoke of would lead voters toward the DC, not the PCI. the irony of the historic compromise Not only was the PCI suddenly forced to defend, in the name of the Historic Compromise, unpopular government policies such as the partial elimination of the scala mobile, rising costs of living due to inflationary monetary policy, and a partial dismantling of the gains earned by the unions during the previous round of labor militancy; it also faced internal dissatisfaction. There was widespread confusion among the Party: “From the start, much of the PCI membership was surprised and confused by the historic compromise; many were jolted when the leadership proposed an alliance with a political force that had been seen as the enemy for so long.” (4) According to Lucio Magri, author of the Tailor of Ulm and one of the founders of Manifesto, a leftwing journal that split from and ultimately rejoined the PCI, “If anything, younger and more combative sections of the population, less accustomed to discipline and delegation, wanted to participate in decision-making and to see the results sooner rather than later.” (5) This internal confusion was aggravated following the election because, “The PCI constituencies expected the party to use its leverage to push through far-reaching reforms. Instead the leadership devoted all its efforts to working out a formal agreement with the DC, backing down on major issues to keep negotiations going…the DC passed a series of measures that served its own interests…raising prices for the basic consumer goods, public transportation, and utilities; and dismantling the cost of living escalator mechanism (scala mobile), which protected the organized working class against inflation.” (6) Here were the perils of being a junior coalition partner. The PCI was not in government but because of the Historic Compromise was forced to defend policies that undermined its own position among its constituents in the name of a broader goal: namely, to demonstrate its “fitness” to govern. Even those elements within the Party that supported the Historic Compromise, according to Magri, were expecting reform but received only defence of the status quo, “Even those convinced of the rightness of Berlinguer’s project not only hoped for but willed a profound change in economic and social policy, and in Italy’s international position, mode of governance and distribution of power. A compromise maybe – but not subaltern cohabitation.” (7) the road not taken Was this the only path available to Berlinguer? Some both on the left and among disinterested historians saw another potential avenue that could have been pursued but was not explored; a Left Unity Coalition between the PCI and the Italian Socialist Party (PSI) – and smaller Left parties. An effective electoral coalition depended both on ideological unity and a program focused on the desires of the PCI base; namely, defense of the scala mobile and living standards of the popular classes, and an end to the corruption identified as a by-product of DC rule. Both the PCI and the official newspaper of the Italian Socialist Party, Avanti, regularly called out the corruption of the DC. The prospective coalition would also have entailed a defense of NATO, but with a varied foreign policy that at times would have been at odds with the NATO’a wider positions, for example, leaning on traditionally good relations between Italy and the Arab Republics. (8) Historian Paul Ginsborg notes that “…the country was crying out for change and reform. It would not be possible to achieve either by making an alliance with the DC. Berlinguer, it is argued, should have capitalized upon the enduring movement of protest in civil society in order to forge an alternative to Christian Democrat politics entirely.” (9) The PCI could not have taken power immediately, but it could have used the years after 1976 to build a united opposition, and to prepare the terrain for a decisive victory at the next elections.” (10) This suggests a qualitatively different view of the potential for the democratic transition in a bourgeois republic. While it was not realistic for a Left Coalition to assume power in 1976, the process of unity coalition building could have served as a vehicle for the consolidation of the Left into a more viable alternative pole in Italian politics. Nor did the PSI represent the only available alliance partner. There was as well the New Left which existed in various forms, ultimately to be joined by the explosive mixture of new social actors and popular demands that emerged on the scene with the Movement of ‘77. the italian new left To the Left of the PCI was a nebulous group organized around a handful of prominent thinkers such as Mario Tronti, Antonio Negri, and Silvia Federici. While their positions can be considered generally Left, they varied significantly on who or what constituted the proletarian class or revolutionary subject. Loosely, they agreed upon a broad conception of politics that placed the organization of the working class as something to be pursued outside of the boundaries of established organizations such as existing trade unions and the Communist or Socialist Parties. For this reason they adopted “Autonomia” (Autonomy) as the label for a body of wide ranging Marxist thought. Alongside this creative application of Marxism were numerous other ideological projects that embraced a variety of ideologies and identities; together they occupied a nebulous space best defined as the “New Left”. While there were numerous periodicals and journals such as Potere Operaio, Primo Maggio, Quaderni Rossi, etc. that all expressed different currents of thought to the left of the PCI, we can view the New Left coalition party, Proletarian Democracy (DP) as the primary organization in question, at least with regards to electoral matters. In the 1976 election the party received approximately 550,000 votes which earned it 6 Members of Parliament. (11) While not decisive, they represented a viable left-wing ally that when taken together with the Socialists at 9% would have allowed for the emergence of a Left Coalition in Parliament that the DC would have had to accommodate in some fashion, even as broader ideological unity was explored. The PCI’s refusal to engage with the New Left could be understood as a combination of old sectarianism and a fundamental misunderstanding or inability to recognize the new insurgent populations that defined the New Left. It is no coincidence that only several months later, after the elections, the Movement of ‘77 exploded onto the scene of Italian politics, expressing many different tendencies and modes of thought, but overall frustration with the existing political status quo, including the PCI. Magri summarizes the composition of the Movement of ‘77: “It was mainly a protest movement in a period of general downturn, mostly driven by anger and disappointment, and kindling huge hopes for a new world…its social base was new and heterogeneous: various marginal groups (unemployed youth, rank and file union activists in the railway and health sectors, jobless graduates), clustered together, or tried to cluster, around the students, whereas industrial workers were neither much in evidence nor the class centrally at issue in the protests.” (12) Clearly, this heterogeneous movement was far from being composed of the PCI’s traditional base, that is the industrial working class. But it represented exactly the constituency for a broader Left alliance against the Center and Right. It could be seen then that the failure of the PCI to extend a meaningful hand to the New Left for the Election of 1976 was a profound error. The Party’s aversion to ideological compromise, its unwillingness to cede ideological and organizational control of the coalition, was fatal. Of course, it also reflected the Party’s opportunism in seeking to secure a grand alliance with the DC. the politics of the possible Was the Left Unity Coalition realistic? The experience of the prodigal Manifesto group which had split from the PCI in the 1960s to form an independent Marxist journal and returned by the late 1970s and the Proletarian Unity Party for Communism which experienced a similar trajectory, both demonstrate that small ideologically left dissident factions were able to dissolve and return to the PCI proper. This suggests a degree of underlying compatibility. Ironically the PCI by refusing to pursue a meaningful alliance with the wider forces of the left contradicted Togliatti’s own thoughts regarding parliament, “In the second place, it is necessary for the parties that fight for socialism, and the communist parties in the front rank of them, to be strong, numerous, well organised and for them to know how to work and fight in such a way as to win a decisive influence in the decisive strata of the working class and the people. In the third place, it is necessary for these parties to be united in their action, because this not only increases their numerical weight…but can allow them to establish a reciprocal understanding and a collaboration with those political forces that are not hostile to social reforms of a socialist type and to a consequent policy of peace.” (13) Furthermore, had the PCI been basing their perception of the role of parliament in 1976 on the broad call for democratic unity advanced by Togliatti – following the logic of the Historic Compromise itself – the unity of the PCI, PSI, DP, and Italian Social Democratic Party (PSDI) could have been pursued under the wide umbrella of anti-imperialism and in defense of democratic values. There also existed a degree of popular support for this position, reported in Avanti.. A press conference of neighborhood leaders appearing in the Party’s official organ indicated that there also was a degree of PSI support for a broader understanding of the left. (14) The Socialist leadership around De Martino could have been approached by the PCI to draft a new unity program to create an alternative center-left coalition. Martino himself advanced a lukewarm but open position at the PSI party congress of 1976, stating in his address to the Party that it was critical that the PSI consider a left-wing alternative politics and observed that some elements within the Party were insisting that the PSI declare they would not join any government without the PCI. (15) While retaining a desire for autonomy and flexibility going into the election, De Martino recognized that the primary strategic goal of the PSI was, “to build a leftwing alliance and alternative.” The failure of the PCI then is not that it rejected an immediate electoral alternative based on alliance with the PSI, but that it did not, after the election, devote energy to constructing a long-term autonomous left alliance that could in time replace the DC. The difficulties in synthesizing a Left Unity Coalition among the PCI, PSI, New Left, and Others were significant. They represented notable differences in viewpoints regarding many issues. However, given the growing popular dissatisfaction with the DC, historic inter-party relations particularly between the PCI and PSI was not impossible. Ginsborg highlights that, while difficult, the decision to not pursue a Left-Unity Coalition would have fateful consequences as, “In the summer of 1976 the opportunity, albeit fraught with difficulty, existed for building an alternative to the Christian Democrats. The opportunity was not taken, and no such chance was to present itself again. the italian lesson What does the Italian General Election of 1976 teach us about the potential rise of Socialist Governance in the United States in the wake of the 2026 Midterm Elections? The 2026 Midterms are not the Italian General Election in 1976. Unlike the PCI which was a well organized, disciplined, national political force, the DSA is still a pre-party formation employing primarily democratic electoral infrastructure to contest specific races. While the PCI could rely upon professional cadre to coordinate national efforts, the DSA is composed primarily of volunteers. Like the General Elections in 1976 Italy, the DSA has made a tremendous breakthrough, relatively speaking, with six candidates being elected to federal office and numerous downballot or endorsed victories. (16) Despite this success, the DSA remains fundamentally subordinate to the Democratic Party. Because of the need to oppose the Republican Party and the still relatively marginal position of the Socialist Movement in the USA, the DSA like the PCI, is compelled to support policy packages pushed by the Democrats that are fundamentally antithetical to a Socialist vision for the United States. But the DSA may suffer should their bourgeois partners, who constitute the actual power in government, pursue policies that undermine the DSA. To combat the effect of being tied to a larger bourgeois force, the DSA must expand its political imagination which the PCI refused to do. It is imperative that socialists seize the mandate offered by voters and propose meaningful reforms to meet immediate material expectations. Simultaneously, it is possible to begin an ideological process of Left Coalition Building which may mean that while a still marginal force in 2026, the DSA enters 2028 and beyond as an independent political party capable of advancing the socialist project and vision that motivates its membership. To speak of coalition building is also to highlight the stark difference between the possibilities open to the PCI that do not exist in the same measure for DSA. Unfortunately, there are no comparably sized overtly Socialist parties that the DSA can join hands with to create the beginning of a coalition. That said, there are options the DSA can cultivate. Third parties such as the Greens, Working Families Party, and others who are not explicitly Socialist could unite with the DSA in a Popular Democratic Coalition; or at least on specific initiatives like the Green New Deal or Cost of Living, that might prepare the ground for later and broader convergence. Similarly there is the possibility of establishing an explicitly political alliance with progressive and independent elements of organized labor. This would be distinct from the broad imperative of supporting the unions as vehicles for securing tangible gains for working people and would represent an effort to create a specific political project transitioning from solely economic initiatives towards broader related challenges. Progressive Democrats are seemingly a potential coalition partner but represent an acute danger for the DSA. They are exactly the mechanism by which the DSA can be maneuvered into supporting candidates and policies that undermine the position of the DSA which could include continued support for Zionism, continued “legal” deportations, or continued funding for foreign wars. That said, Progressive Democrats could be persuaded to provide indirect material support for the DSA by channeling funds and resources to DSA initiatives. This does not amount to joining a formal Popular Democratic Coalition, but nonetheless could help. The common thread running through all of these options is the necessity for the Popular Democratic Coalition to have a specific end goal in mind. Unity for the sake of unity was not viable nor beneficial for the PCI nor would it be viable for the DSA.
